statements.text: This is why we need to encourage people developing or deploying AI systems to be thoughtful about what they are putting out into the world. We must develop the tools, methodologies, and standards to ensure that AI products and services are safe and secure, accurate, free of harmful bias, and otherwise trustworthy.
statements.context: Opening statement by the Subcommittee on Research and Technology chair at a congressional hearing on managing AI risks.

statements.text: But I don't know if that's really the question now, is it, you know, in terms of improving these outcomes with AI? [...] is it the Turing test that that we should be focused on or what is the question that we should be focused on with the fair implementation of AI across a multitude of sectors that are determining our economy at grand scale with 5 seconds left?
statements.context: House Science Committee hearing on 'Trustworthy AI: Managing the Risks of Artificial Intelligence,' during a Q&A exchange in the Chairwoman's final seconds.

statements.text: So in 2019, NIST developed the strategy for Federal engagement in developing technical standards and tools for artificial intelligence. [...] what was included in this strategy and why it is important that we have strategies for engaging in the development of technical standards for artificial intelligence.
statements.context: House Subcommittee hearing on trustworthy AI, first round of questions with the chair recognizing herself.

statements.text: this is a leadership moment for the United States of America. And we are going to shape how the world's going to go on this. [...] It's not just the question of harm, but it's also the questions of, you know, the meta challenges that come before us that are somewhat brought on by AI. It's forcing us to be more collaborative.
statements.context: Closing remarks by the subcommittee chair at the end of a House hearing on trustworthy AI.

statements.text: These systems are now deployed across every sector of our society and economy, including education, law enforcement, medicine, and transportation. These are sectors for which AI carries the potential for both great benefit, and great harm.
statements.context: Prepared statement of Chairwoman Johnson submitted for the record during a House Science Committee hearing on trustworthy AI.

statements.text: We parallel track our charge, we parallel track our effort, because artificial intelligence is here. This is maybe, in part, why I have a master's in philosophy and social policy, because it is raising unbelievable philosophical questions, artificial intelligence. It is not these gimmick podcasts that are just talking about falling in love with a robot or your kids doing homework with the AI chat. That is all interesting and disruptive. [...] A regulatory framework would help.
statements.context: Floor speech by Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI) during a one-hour special order covering industrial policy, supply chains, quantum computing, and AI.

statements.text: our Federal Government has got to serve as a good steward and partner of the technology proliferation through the guardrails that Dr. Chowdhury is talking about or our lunch will be eaten. [...] what do you think are the biggest cross-national problems in need of global oversight with regard to artificial intelligence right now?
statements.context: House hearing on artificial intelligence where Rep. Stevens asks a witness about international AI oversight.

statements.text: And then we've got this AI situation going on. [...] I asked them about convening international actors to put into place these guardrails, particularly as our ranking member showcased some of the nefarious ways in which the CCP is using AI.
statements.context: House Science Committee hearing on U.S. leadership in critical and emerging technologies.

statements.text: We need to enforce watermarking, this technique of putting secret information in AI-generated output so we can detect when it's generated by AI.
statements.context: Witness testimony at a hearing on AI and the Department of Energy's role in U.S. competitiveness and security.

statements.text: I was especially pleased to see the National Institute of Standards and Technology released the AI risk management Framework in January, an important step in AI safety that was developed by the 2020 National AI Initiative Act, a Science Committee product.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Haley Stevens at a joint House Science Committee hearing on AI risk management.

statements.text: And, Mr. Watney, I was obviously excited to see you mention in your testimony privacy, preserving machine learning. [...] And look, this is why we're excited about the PET bill, the Privacy Enhancing Technology Research Act.
statements.context: Subcommittee hearing on AI risk management featuring expert testimony, where the representative references pending privacy legislation.

statements.text: Unfortunately, so too are its risks – not just the hypothetical but very much the here and now.
statements.context: Opening statement by Ranking Member Haley Stevens at a joint House Science Subcommittee hearing on AI risk management.

statements.text: I look forward to learning more about how the pilot program is proceeding, how the program brings together federal and non-government partners, and how it can inform a potential full-scale NAIRR program.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Ranking Member Haley Stevens at a joint Science Subcommittee hearing on federal science agencies and AI's role in scientific discovery.

statements.text: I am proud that we led the development of the 2020 National AI Initiative Act to accelerate and coordinate Federal investments in research, standards, and education in trustworthy AI. In that Act, Congress built upon existing National Science Foundation and Department of Energy AI research and education programs, including authorizing NSF to lead the National AI Research Institutes program.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Rep. Haley Stevens at a joint House Science Committee hearing on AI and scientific discovery.

statements.text: What the Privacy Enhancing Technology Research Act gets us is an opportunity to further strengthen and utilize Federal agencies to regulate our artificial intelligence.
statements.context: House floor speech introducing H.R. 4755, the Privacy Enhancing Technology Research Act, during a pro forma legislative session.

statements.text: Do any of you have thoughts on the role of AI in facilitating not only finance but also financial regulation and oversight?
statements.context: Remarks at a policy event on AI innovation in financial services, with a lawmaker questioning panelists on AI's regulatory applications.

statements.text: I think national right-sized frameworks. I mean, we rely a lot on the risk AI management framework, and so anything that has a consistent baseline for all of our States will help us.
statements.context: Remarks at a financial services AI policy event.

statements.text: The budget for the Fiscal Year 2026, it slashed NIST funding by $325 million, $325 million dollars. And we're eliminating 500 jobs from the agency's lab program. You know, we know, so many of us, how sacred this work is and how important it is, even when you just have just a handful of researchers working on these matters. And the cuts hinder NIST's AI-related efforts. They're going to weaken cybersecurity and privacy standards, something I have legislation on, and limit advanced manufacturing, physical infrastructure, and resilience innovation.
statements.context: Congressional hearing on implementing the Administration's AI Action Plan, featuring OSTP Director Kratsios as witness.

statements.text: The President’s Fiscal Year 2026 budget slashes NIST’s funding by $325 million and eliminates over 500 jobs from the agency’s lab program.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Haley Stevens at a Research and Technology Subcommittee hearing on the Administration's AI Action Plan.
